water was being drained out through their land. The administration had 
cautioned the villagers living downstream not to go near the flooded rivulet 
or artificial lake until the situation becomes normal. 
 Landslide at Swarghat Bilaspur : Heavy rain caused massive damage to 
private and public property in District Bilaspur on 18th August, 2019. This 
was the highest ever rainfall in 24 hours. All 12 districts received excess 
rainfall with Bilaspur topping the list with 252 mm, which is 2,586 percen t 
more than normal. Himachal Pradesh on 18th August, 2019 received 102.5 
mm of rainfall, 1,065 percent more than normal in a single day. In District 
Bilaspur the major roads were either blocked due to landslides or due to 
caving in of portions of roads. Th e National Highway from Swarghat to 
Bilaspur was blocked due to landslide at various spots and tourists were 
trapped since last 18 hours. 
The District Administration had started rescue operation early in the 
morning through water boats. 2000 passengers were stuck in between 
Swarghat Bilaspur road. 267 persons were evacuated through water boats 
and were dropped at Luhnu Ground, Bilaspur. Food packets and drinking 
water were served to them, and two ambulances were also deployed there. 
From Luhnu Ground pass engers were dropped at Bus Stand, Bilaspur 
through HRTC buses. In this situation, Village Disaster Management 
Committee (VDMC) of Village Charrol and Jamli also played a vital role in 
rescuing the affected passe ngers. They also provided food, water and 
necessary amenities to people. For rehabilitation, District Admi nistration 
and VDMC’s member arranged stay for affected persons in Govt. Sr. Sec. 
School, Jamli and in Mahajan Niwas. District Administration has gone an 
immediate relief to the affected passenge rs and made considerable efforts 
to rehabilitate them. 
 Building Collapse at Kumarhatti- Nahan Road: On 14 July 2019 , at around 
3.45 PM a multi -storied building (Sahaj Tandoori Dhaba) located toward s 
valley side near Kumarhatti Junction on Kumarhatti -Nahan National Highway 
No. 907 in District Solan collapsed , due to heavy rains killing 14 persons. 
Immediate action for response was taken by the District Administration with 
the help of local Police, Home Guards, Fire Services, Indian Army and CRPF. 
Simultaneously, NDRF was also requested to support ongoing rescue work to 
use their expertise in collapsed structure search and rescue. Two teams of 
NDRF from Panchkula and Sunni, Shimla were mobilized by the evening.

3. Structures damaged: Due to the current disaster , a number of 
houses and others assets suffered moderate to severe damages. 
The details are as under:-

4. Damage to roads: 
 Roads are life lines of the S tate as there are virtually negligible 
modes of alternate transport. The economy of S tate which comprises 
mainly tourism and horticu lture is highly dependent upon road 
infrastructure. Himachal Pradesh has vast network of roads, which 
comprises 33876 km. of State Roads and 3017 km. of National 
Highways. The monsoon season has played havoc with road 
infrastructure this year. Extensiv e damages to the roads have been 
inflicted by way of landslides , damages to the various structures like 
Retaining walls, Breast walls, Cross drainage works, Bridges, besides 
heavy damage to the pavement/riding surface. It is mainly attributed 
to the mountainous/steep terrain and fragile Geological strata in most 
part of the S tate triggering landslides. The climate change/global 
warming has resulted in non uniform distribution of rains with very 
high intensity rainfall in localized areas thus, aggravating t he extent of 
damages to road infrastructure. As a result , a number of road 
stretches, culverts and other structures have been washed away 
especially in Districts of Chamba, Shimla, Kinnaur & Bilaspur. The 
department has deployed adequate number of various types of 
machinery including excavators, tippers, dozers and manpower as per 
requirement to restore the traffic in shortest possible time to provide 
relief to the general public at large. Nearly 23905 km of road leng th 
has been adversely affected. Due to flash flood and landslide, the 
PWD Infrastructure i.e. Roads, Bridges and culverts ha ve been

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2019
text:
Page No. 23 

severely damaged during the current Mo nsoon se ason. The total 
losses on this account have been assessed as Rs. 594.99Cr. 
(Annexure-II). The damaged road infrastructure has been restored 
immediately with the help of Government and private machinery in 
order to avoid inconvenience to public. The permanent restoration 
work is still in progress. 
5. Damage to Irrigation and water supply schemes: 

 Irrigation & Public Health Department is maintaining 9516 
Water Supply, 2669 Irrigation and 20 sewerage schemes in Rural and 
Urban areas of the State, The department is also protecting the flood 
prone areas to save culturable land, public and private property by 
providing flood protection measures in the shape of embankments, 
spurs and wire crates etc. 
 There had been heavy rain fall in various parts of the State 
during the monsoon season -2019. Heavy loss to the Government 
infrastructure as well as to the I&PH Schem es in the State has been 
reported. The heavy rains have led huge damages to the Water 
Supply, Irrigation, sewerage and flood control works of the 
Department. Majority of water supply and irrigation schemes have 
sources in Khuds/ Nallah/ Rivers, which got damaged due to heavy 
floods. At many places rains triggered landslides and washed the 
I&PH schemes and other common assets. 
 In many places flash flood water entered in the campus of 
pump houses resulting in silting of pump houses, Treatment plants, 
pumping machinery etc. This necessitated repair/cleaning of pumping 
machinery, cleaning /de-silting of Pump Houses & other structures. In 
some places Gravity Mains/Rising mains have also been washed 
away/damaged due to landslides. 
 Being ess ential service first priority has been given to 
restore Water Supply and Irrigation Schemes in a time bound manner 
and all damaged water supply and Irrigation schemes have been 
restored temporarily. Pipes damaged due to heavy rains/ landslides 
have been re placed out of un -utilized pipes available in the 
departmental stores which were procured for ongoing schemes.

works for the year 2019 -20. For permanent restoration of all 
damaged schemes funds of Rs 285.92 crore shall be required.

 Irrigation schemes- 1519 Nos. 
Total loss has been estimated till date as Rs. 321.26 Crore. 
(Annexure-III) 

6. Damage to Agriculture Crops: 
 Due to the current disaster, the crops have been affected to 
some extent. As per the first assessment of damages caused to 
standing Kharif crops because of heavy rains in the S tate, the overall 
loss to crops in terms of money value as assessed is R s. 52.77 crores. 
The cultivated land has also been damaged/washed away due to 
siltation/landslides/cloudbrust and loss in terms of money value is 
around Rs. 34.74 crores. Therefore, the total loss to agriculture crop 
and cultivated lands due to heavy rains is estimated about Rs. 87.51 
crores. The losses calculated as per the norms on the area where crop 
loss is more than 33% comes to Rs. 3.24 crores and the loss to 
washed away cultivated area is Rs. 12.05 cores. 
(Appendix –IVA,IVB ). 

7. Damage to Horticultural Crops: 
 Horticulture is an important sector of economic development 
in the S tate, which is contributing around 5000 crore towards S tates 
economy. It has a capacity to generate more income and 
employment per unit area. Fruit crops occupy about 2.29 lakh Ha 
area in the state (2016 -17). Apple, Mango, Citrus and other stone 
fruits are major fruit crops grown in the S tate and constitute about 
83 % of total fruit production. Apple is th e dominating fruit crop of

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2019
text:
Page No. 25 

the State occupying about 48% of the total area under fruits & about 
76.50 % o f the total production and the S tate earned its name as 
“Apple State of India” is marching forward as “Fruit bowl of India”. 
About 5 lac families are directly or indirectly involved in the 
Horticulture primarily fr uit production & its allied activities viz Bee 
Keeping, Mushroom production, Floriculture and Fruit processing. 
State economy is likely is shoot up in a big way as far as Horticulture 
industry is concerned with the launching of World Bank -aided-HP 
Horticulture Development Project and Asian Development Bank 
aided HP Sub -Tropical Development Project worth Rs. 1134.00 crore 
and Rs. 1688.0 crore respectively in which specific emphasis is to be 
given for High Density Plantation of various crops, creation of ampl e 
water resources through available means & strengthening of 
infrastructure facilities which are considered to be vital for 
promotion of horticulture in the entire State. 
 During the past couple of years , the S tate is witnessing 
natural fury/ calam ities at intermittent intervals particularly losses 
being inflicted during the monsoon season resulting thereby the 
fluctuating production and productivity of fruit crops. Major losses 
generally inflicted during the monsoon season are losses in the form 
of mortality of young nursery plants due to constant water 
stagnation, partial damage to the twigs of fruit trees, landslides in 
various areas, quantitative and qualitative losses. Qualitative losses 
are more oftenly high due to appearance of various disease s in 
general as due to excessive rains diseases spread in alarming 
proportion thereby affecting the marketing of the produce. Size and 
colour of developing fruits is also affected greatly if rains are 
torrential. 
 During the current disaster losses to fruit crops to the tune 
of Rs. 34.35 Crores and land washed away Rs. 11.55 Cr. as per the 
norms of GOI were occurred ( Annexure IVD ). Similarly, the actual 
losses to fruit crops during rainy season were Rs. 10.69 C rores 
(Annexure IVC).

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DAMAGES DUE TO CLOUDBURST, FLASH -FLOODS 
AND LANDSLIDES DURING MONSOON, 2020. 

State Profile 

Physical Location: 

Himachal Pradesh is predominantly a mountainous State located in North – West 
India. It shares an international border w ith China. The State has highly dissected 
mountain ranges interspersed with deep gorges 
and valleys. It is also characterized with diverse 
climate that varies from semi tropical in lower hills, 
to semi arctic in the cold deserts areas of Spiti and 
Kinnaur. Altitude ranges from 350 meters to 6975 
meters above mean sea level. It is located between 
Latitude 30 O 22’.40” N to 33 O 12’.20” N and 
Longitude 75O 45’.55” E to 79O 04’.20” E. 
Demography: 
Population of Himachal Pradesh is 68.56 lakh 
persons as per the Census report for the year 2011. 
89.01% of the total population inhabits 20,604 
villages in the rural areas of the State. These 
villages are sparsely distributed across the State 
having population density as low as 1 -2 persons 
per square kilometer in the re mote and tribal area 
of Lahaul & Spiti, Hamirpur district has largest population density of 369 persons per 
square kilometer as against 123 persons per square kilometer for the whole State. 
Himachal Pradesh is one of the few states of the country where gen der equality is an 
integral part of the social ethos as well as the overall development strategy. Female 
literacy is well above the national level and women employment is much higher than 
in most states of the country.

Administrative Units: 
In order to make the functioning smooth, the State is divided into twelve districts 
which are grouped in three Revenue Divisions i.e. Shimla, Mandi and Kangra. There 
are 71 Sub Di visions, 106 Tehsil, 63 Sub -Tehsil, 79 Development Blocks and 3226 
Panchayats. The State has very effective structure of PRI’s comprising 12 Zila 
Parishads and 78 Panchayat Samitis. There are also 30 Municipal Councils and 23 
Nagar Panchayats, besides 7 C antonment Boards and 2 Municipal Corporation in the 
State. 
Topography: 
Topographically, the state can be divided into three zones: 
1. The Shiwaliks or Outer Himalayas: It covers the lower hills of Kangra, 
Hamirpur, Una and Bilaspur, lower parts of Mandi, Sola n and Sirmour districts. 
Within this zone, altitude varies from 350 m to 1500 m. 

2. Inner Himalayas or mid -mountains: Altitude varies from 1500 m to 4500 m 
above mean sea level and includes areas such as the upper parts of Pachhad and 
Renuka in Sirmaur distr ict, Chachiot and Karsog tehsils of Mandi district and 
upper parts of Churah tehsil of Chamba district. 

3. Alpine zone or the greater Himalayas: Has altitude above 4500 m above 
mean sea level and comprises areas of Kinnaur district, Pangi tehsil of Chamba 
district and area of Lahaul & Spiti district. 

Geology & Geomorphology: 
Himachal Pradesh with its complex geological structures presents a complicated 
topography with intricate mosaic of 
mountainous ranges, hills and valleys. 
Composed of recent Alluvium, Sh iwalik hills 
are made up of rocks such as sandstone, 
shale and clay that came into existence 
during the Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene 
period. 
The central part that extends from Chamba 
district in the north to Shimla district in the 
south is ma inly represented by Jatog group 
of rocks which originated in middle 
Proterozoic period. In the north eastern 
portion unclassified Granites borders the 
central part in between Kullu, eastern 
Shimla, Lahaul Spiti and parts of Kinnaur 
Figure 1.2 Geography of Himachal Pradesh

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2020
text:
Page No. 4 

district. The eastern greater Himalaya presents the Triassic formation which is found 
in Kaza tehsil of Lahaul Spiti district. The oldest rocks are Granites found atJeori -
Wangtu and Bandel near Largi in Kullu district. These granites date back to a stage of 
the crust at a time wh en India was located 8000 Km southwest of its present 
position. 

Climate: 
The climate varies across the state with the altitude. In the southern low tracks 
between an altitude of 400 -900 it is hot sub humid type, between 900 -1800m 
altitude warm & te mperate, between 900 -2400 m 
cool & temperate, cold alpine & glacial above 
2400-4800 m altitude. Bilaspur, Kangra, Mandi, 
Sirmour, and Una districts experience sub tropical 
monsoon, mild and dry winter and hot summer. 
Shimla district has tropical upland typ e climate 
with mild and dry winter and short warm summer. 
Chamba district experiences, humid subtropical 
type climate having mild winter, long hot summer 
and moist all season. Kullu district experience 
mainly humid subtropical type of climate with 
mild winter moist all season, long hot summer and 
marine. During the period from January to 
February heavy snowfall in higher reaches create 
conditions for low temperature throughout the 
state making it unpleasant and series of western 
disturbances also affect the state.

Detailed Report on Current Disaster-Damages and Losses 

 (a) Extent of Monsoon, 2020: 
 This year, the South-west monsoon in Himachal Pradesh arrived on 24 th of 
June 2020. Monsoon withdrawn from entire state of HP on 30th September 2020. 
Normal date of withdrawal of monsoon from the HP is 25 th September. During 
this Monsoon Season, 567.2 mm rainfall was recorded in Himachal Pra desh, 
which is 26% below the Long Period Average value. Out of twelve districts of the 
state, 3 districts (Bilaspur ( 9%), Kullu (05%), Una (10%) received normal rainfall 
and eight district received deficient rainfall.One districts viz Lahaul and Spiti ( -
73%) received scanty rainfall during the monsoon season – 2020. For details 
report, please see Table-1. Last year i.e. in year 2019, Monsoon was withdrawn 
from Himachal Pradesh on 11 th October 2019 with a Cumulative rainfall of 685.5 
mm which was 10% less fr om LPA value. A comparison of Monsoon Rainfall and 
Withdrawal dates for previous years is given in Table-2.

 (b.) Weather summery for the month of September 2020 (i.e. 01 ST 
September to 30th September) 
Cumulative Rainfall during this year in the month of September 2020 is 29.9 
mm which was below normal by 77% over the state as a whole. Highest rainfall 
viz 269.8 mm (+93%) was recorded in HP during September 2018. and Lowest 
rainfall viz 29.9 mm ( -77) was recorded in 2020, followed by 38.5 mm ( -71%) 
in 2004. Out of twelve district, all districts received either scanty or deficient 
rainfall in the month of September (please see table-3 for details). There were only 
2 spells (04th & 07th Sept) of rainfall during current monsoon season ( September 
2020) in Himachal Pradesh. Rest of the September was either dry or received very 
less rainfall that at few places spread over the State. On 04 th September 2020, 
Rainfall: Sarkaghat: 83.0 mm, Nurpur: 81.0 mm, Nahan: 43.7 mm. On 07 th 
September 2020, Rainfall: Gohar=48.0 mm, Ghumarwin=30.0 mm, 
Hamirpur=28.0 mm. Highest Maximum Temperature of 38.6 oC was recorded at 
Una on 21.09.2020 & minimum temperature of 3.3 oC was recorded in Keylong 
on 27.09.2020. Percentage (%) departure of precipitation in the month of 
September for previous years are mentioned in table-4.

3) Structures damaged: Due to the current disaster, a number of 
houses and others assets suffered moderate to severe 
damages. The details are as under:- 
 10 Nos fully damaged Pucca and 135 Nos. Kucha houses = 145 
 61 Nos Severly damaged Pucca & 483 Nos. Kucha houses = 544 
 Cowshed, gharats, shops and labor sheds = 618 
Total - 1307 
 Loss on this account has been assessed as Rs. 8.58 Cr. 
Details is at Appendix-VII i.e. Specific format as prescribed by 
NDM division of MHA, GOI. 

4) Damage to Roads, Bridges and Culverts: 
 Roads are life line of the S tate as there are virtually negligible 
modes of alter nate transport. The economy of S tate which 
comprises mainly tourism and horticulture is highly depend ent 
upon road infrastructure. Himachal Pradesh has vast network of 
roads, which comprises 33876 km. of State Roads and 3017 km. 
of National Highways. The monsoon season played havoc with 
road infrastructure this year. Extensive damages to the roads 
have been inflicted by way of landslides, damages to the various 
structures like retaining walls, breast walls, cross drainage works, 
bridges, besides heavy damage to the pavement/riding surface. It 
is mainly attributed to the mountai nous/steep terrain and fr agile 
geological strata in most part of the S tate triggering landslides. 
The climate change/global warming has resulted in non uniform 
distribution of rains with very high intensity rainfall in localized 
areas thus, aggravating the extent of damages to ro ad 
infrastructure. As a result , a number of road stretches, culverts 
and other structures have been washed away especially in 
Districts of Chamba, Shimla, Kinnaur & Bilaspur. The department 
deployed adequate number of various types of machinery 
including e xcavators, tippers, dozers and manpower as per 
requirement to restore the traffic in shortest possible time to

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2020
text:
Page No. 15 

provide relief to the general public at large. Nearly 25033.54 km 
of road leng th has been adversely affected. Due to flash flood 
and landslid e, the PWD Infrastructure i.e. roads, b ridges and 
culverts ha ve been severe ly damaged during the current 
Monsoon se ason. The total losses on this account ha s been 
assessed as Rs. 432.50 Cr. Detail is at Annexure-D. 
 The damaged road infrastructure has been r estored 
immediately with the help of Government and private machinery 
in order to avoid inconvenience to public. Pucca road – 13,600 
Kms, Kutcha Road-11400.54 Kms, Bridges – 20 Nos. and Culverts 
– 197 Nos. got damaged and The State has incurred liability to the 
effect and payments need to be made. The permanent 
restoration work is still in progress. 
 To restore road connectivity, 1357 Nos. of JCBs of Public Work 
Department and 3846 Nos of JCBs were hired from private 
agencies, 241 dossers, 1210 T ippers were deployed to clear 
roads. 

5) Damage to Irrigation and water supply schemes: 
 Jal Shakti Vibhag is maintaining 9516 Water Supply, 
2669 Irrigation and 20 sewerage schemes in Rural and Urban 
areas of the State, The department is also protectin g the flood 
prone areas to save culturable land, public and private property 
by providing flood protection measures in the shape of 
embankments, spurs and wire crates etc. 
 There had been heavy rain fall in various parts of the 
State during the monsoon sea son-2020. Heavy loss to the 
Government infrastructure as well as to the Jal Shakti Schemes in 
the State has been reported. The heavy rains have led huge 
damages to the Water Supply, Irrigation, sewerage and flood 
control works of the Department. Majority of water supply and 
irrigation schemes have sources in Khuds/ Nallah/ Rivers, which 
got damaged due to heavy floods. At many places rains triggered 
landslides and washed the I&PH schemes and other common 
assets.

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2020
text:
Page No. 16 

 In many places flash flood water entered in the campus 
of pump houses resulting in silting of pump houses, Treatment 
plants, pumping machinery etc. This necessitated repair/cleaning 
of pumping machinery, cleaning /de -silting of Pump Houses & 
other structures. In some places Gravity Mains/Rising m ains have 
also been washed away/damaged due to landslides. 
 Being essential service first priority has been given to 
restore Water Supply and Irrigation Schemes in a time bound 
manner and all damaged water supply and Irrigation schemes 
have been restored temporarily. Pipes damaged due to heavy 
rains/ landslides have been replaced out of un -utilized pipes 
available in the departmental stores which were procured for 
ongoing schemes. 
 In order to repair /restore the damaged W ater Supply & 
Irrigation Schemes a sum of Rs. 72.77 crore has been spent out of 
the funds available for operation and maintenance of 
schemes/capital works for the year 20 20-21. For permanent 
restoration of all damaged schemes funds of Rs 330.65 crore shall 
be required. 

 Following schemes of Jal Shakti Vibhag were 
significantly affected, due to the current disaster. The damage 
recorded is given below: 
 Urban Water Supply – 268 Nos. 
 Rural Water Supply – 5487 Nos. 
 Irrigation schemes- 1306 Nos. 
 Flood Control - 151 Nos. 
 Sewerage Scheme-105 Nos. 
 Hand Pump-560 Nos. 
Total loss has been estimated till date at Rs. 330.65 Crore. A 
schemewise detail of damage and losses is at Annexure-E. 

6) Damage to Agriculture Crops: 
 During this monsoon period the pe rcent departure of rainfall 
in the months of April, May, June, July, August and September, 2020 
was to the extent of -25%, -16%, -35%, -28%, 1% and -77%

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2020
text:
Page No. 17 

respectively. About 20% of area is sown in the month of April -May 
whereas 80% of area is sown in the m onth of June which is a peak 
Kharif sowing period. Due to normal rains in most part of the state, 
the sowing could be done on time. However, during Monsoon 
season, 2020 there was heavy rainfall in some pockets of the state 
and standing Kharif crops viz. Ma ize, Paddy, Pulses & Vegetables 
were affected to some extent. The total area of 37360.98 Hectares 
was damaged and 538.75 Hectare land was washed away. The total 
damage including agriculture land damage in terms of money value 
has been assessed around Rs. 16.04 Crores and Crop loss Rs. 61.32 
Crores Details is at Appendix –IVA & IVB i.e. Specific format as 
prescribed by NDM division of MHA, GOI. 

7) Damage to Horticultural Crops: 
 Horticulture is an important sector of economic 
development in the S tate, which is contributing around 5000 
crore towards S tates economy. It has a capacity to generate 
more income and employment per unit area. Fruit crops occupy 
about 2.29 lakh Ha areas in the state (2016 -17). Apple, Mango, 
Citrus and other stone fruits are major fruit crops grown in the 
State and constitute about 83 % of total fruit production. Apple 
is the dominating fruit crop of the S tate occupying about 48% of 
the total area under fruits & about 76.50 % o f the total 
production and the S tate earned its nam e as “Apple State of 
India” is marching forward as “Fruit bowl of India”. About 5 lac 
families are directly or indirectly involved in the Horticulture 
primarily fruit production & its allied activities viz Bee Keeping, 
Mushroom production, Floriculture and Fruit processing. State 
economy is likely is shoot up in a big way as far as Horticulture 
industry is concerned with the launching of World Bank -aided-
HP Horticulture Development Project and Asian Development 
Bank aided HP Sub -Tropical Development Project worth Rs. 
1134.00 crore and Rs. 1688.0 crore respectively in which specific 
emphasis is to be given for High Density Plantation of various 
crops, creation of ample water resources through available

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2020
text:
Page No. 18 

means & strengthening of infrastructure facilities which are 
considered to be vital for promotion of horticulture in the entire 
State. 
 During the past couple of years, the State is witnessing 
natural fury/ calamities at intermittent intervals particularly 
losses being inflicted during the monsoon season resulting 
thereby the fluctuating production and productivity of fruit 
crops. Major losses generally inflicted during the monsoon 
season are losses in the form of mortality of young nursery 
plants due to constant water stagnation, partial damage to the 
twigs of fruit trees, landslides in various areas, quantitative and 
qualitative losses. Qualitative losses are more oftenly high due to 
appearance of various diseases in general as due to excessive 
rains diseases spread in alarming proportion thereby affecti ng 
the marketing of the produce. Size and colour of developing 
fruits is also affected greatly if rains are torrential. 
 During the current disaster losses to fruit crops to the 
tune of Rs. 1.86 Crores and land loss of Rs. 0.71 Cr. has been 
occurred. Details are at Appendix IVC & D i.e. Specific format as 
prescribed by NDM division of MHA, GOI. 

8) Rural Development: A lot of infrastrutre like panchayat ghars, 
Mahila Mandal Bhawans, Community Centers etc. of the Rural 
Development Department have susta ined heavy damages during 
the current disaster. The total loss on this account has been 
assessed to Rs 5.11 Crore Detail of losses and damages is at 
Annexure-F.

State, heavy damages like HT/LT lines, poles & DTR to electrical 
infrastructure occurred and the losses / damages have been 
worked out to the tune of Rs. 5.49 Crore. Detail of losses and 
damages is at Annexure-G.

restoration works remains 20% which are highly insufficient keeping 
in view the extent of damages and losses sustained during Monsoon

to carryout necessary relief and restoration work o f the damaged 
infrastructure is the hilly State.

Page No. 1 

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DAMAGES DUE TO CLOUDBURST, FLASH -FLOODS 
AND LANDSLIDES DURING MONSOON, 2022. 

State Profile 

Physical Location: 

Himachal Pradesh is predominantly a mountainous State located in North – West 
India. It shares an international border with China. The State has highly dissected 
mountain ranges interspersed with deep gorges 
and valleys. It is also characterized with diver se 
climate that varies from semi tropical in lower hills, 
to semi arctic in the cold deserts areas of Spiti and 
Kinnaur. Altitude ranges from 350 meters to 6975 
meters above mean sea level. It is located between 
Latitude 30 O 22’.40” N to 33 O 12’.20” N and 
Longitude 75O 45’.55” E to 79O 04’.20” E. 
Demography: 
Population of Himachal Pradesh is 68.56 lakh 
persons as per the Census report for the year 2011. 
89.01% of the total population inhabits 20,604 
villages in the rural areas of the State. These 
villages are sparsely distributed across the State 
having population density as low as 1 -2 persons 
per square kilometer in the remote and tribal area 
of Lahaul & Spiti, Hamirpur district has largest population density of 369 persons per 
square kilometer as against 123 persons per square kilometer for the whole State. 
Himachal Pradesh is one of the few states of the country where gender equality is an 
integral part of the social ethos as well as the overall development strategy. Female 
literacy is well above the national level and women employment is much higher than 
in most states of the country. 

Figure 1.1Digital Elevation Model, H.P.

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2022
HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2022
text:
Page No. 3 

Administrative Units: 
In order to make the functioning smooth, the State is divided into twelve districts 
which are grouped in three Revenue Divisions i.e. Shimla, Mandi and Kangra. There 
are 71 Sub Divisions, 106 Tehsil, 63 Sub-Tehsil, 79 Development Blocks and 3226 
Panchayats. The State has very effective structure of PRI’s comprising 12 Zila 
Parishads and 78 Panchayat Samitis. There are also 30 Municipal Councils and 23 
Nagar Panchayats, besides 7 Cantonment Boards and 2 M unicipal Corporation in the 
State. 
Topography: 
Topographically, the state can be divided into three zones: 
1. The Shiwaliks or Outer Himalayas: It covers the lower hills of Kangra, 
Hamirpur, Una and Bilaspur, lower parts of Mandi, Solan and Sirmour districts. 
Within this zone, altitude varies from 350 m to 1500 m. 

2. Inner Himalayas or mid -mountains: Altitude varies from 1500 m to 4500 m 
above mean sea level and includes areas such as the upper par ts of Pachhad and 
Renuka in Sirmaur district, Chachiot and Karsog tehsils of Mandi district and 
upper parts of Churah tehsil of Chamba district. 

3. Alpine zone or the greater Himalayas: Has altitude above 4500 m above 
mean sea level and comprises areas of Ki nnaur district, Pangi tehsil of Chamba 
district and area of Lahaul & Spiti district. 

Geology & Geomorphology: 
Himachal Pradesh with its complex geological structures presents a complicated 
topography with intricate mosaic of 
mountainous ranges, hills and valleys. 
Composed of recent Alluvium, Shiwalik hills 
are made up of rocks such as sandstone, 
shale and clay tha t came into existence 
during the Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene 
period. 
The central part that extends from Chamba 
district in the north to Shimla district in the 
south is mainly represented by Jatog group 
of rocks which originated in middle 
Proterozoic period. In the north eastern 
portion unclassified Granites borders the 
central part in between Kullu, eastern 
Shimla, Lahaul Spiti and parts of Kinnaur 
Figure 1.2 Geography of Himachal Pradesh

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2022
text:
Page No. 4 

district. The eastern greater Himalaya presents t he Triassic formation which is found 
in Kaza tehsil of Lahaul Spiti district. The oldest rocks are Granites found atJeori -
Wangtu and Bandel near Largi in Kullu district. These granites date back to a stage of 
the crust at a time when India was located 8000 Km southwest of its present 
position. 

Climate: 
The climate varies across the state with the altitude. In the southern low tracks 
between an altitude of 400 -900 it is hot sub humid type, between 900 -1800m 
altitude warm & temperate, between 900 -2400 m 
cool & temperate, cold alpine & glacial above 
2400-4800 m altitude. Bilaspur, Kangra, Mandi, 
Sirmour, and Una districts experience sub tropical 
monsoon, mild and dry winter and hot summer. 
Shimla district has tropical upland type climate 
with mild and dry winter and short warm summer. 
Chamba district experi ences, humid subtropical 
type climate having mild winter, long hot summer 
and moist all season. Kullu district experience 
mainly humid subtropical type of climate with 
mild winter moist all season, long hot summer and 
marine. During the period from January to 
February heavy snowfall in higher reaches create 
conditions for low temperature throughout the 
state making it unpleasant and series of western 
disturbances also affect the state.

As per Land use statistics, Ministry of Agriculture (GoI ), 2005, about 12.21 percent of 
the total reporting area of 4547000 ha of the state (out of 5567000 ha. of

percent is under the cultivable wasteland, fallow

Five perennial rivers Satluj, Beas, Ravi, Chenab 
and Yamuna flow through the state. The utility of 
these rivers though restricted considerably by 
the rugged and undulating terrain of the State, 
nevertheless, these rivers possess immense 
potential for the generation of h ydro-electricity.

4. Flash flood and landslides triggered by incessant rainfall in 
Himachal Pradesh have caused extensive damage: 
In the flash flood and landslides, 15 people have been killed and 8 are 
missing so far, a couple of bridges including British era chakki Bridge, located 
along Pathankot -Jogindernar rail line in Kangra district, have also been 
washed away while over half a dowen roads incl uding Chandigarh -Manali 
national highway are blocked. 
Heavy rains have caused havoc in Himachal Pradesh since 19 -08-2022 night. 
In the flash floods and landslides, 11 cattle have died wile 8 are missing. 
Across state 14 houses, 5 cowsheds, 6 vehicles and coupe of bridges have 
also ben damaged while 7 roads are closed. 
In Mandi district, 8 member of a family belonging to the Panchayat 
pradhan Khem Singh were killed at Kashan village under Gohar Sub division 
after their house collapsed ni a landslide and all of them got stuck under the 
debris. The district administration with the help of police, NDRF and SDRF 
had launched the rescue operation to save those trapped under the debris. 
District Administration had also reached at the spot but e ven lot of efforts 
family members could not be saved as from the debris only the dead bodies 
were recovered. 
In Mandi district, a flash flood triggered by cloud burst resulted into 
the death of 2 persons and washing away of 5 houses. 
In Hamirpur district, 22 persons were left stranded in the roof top of the 
building near Beas River at Kheiri village under sujanpur tehsil and all were 
rescued by the administration. 
In the state, 3 persons including a woman were killed in Chamba 
district after a house locate d in Banet village of Bhattiyat Tehsil collapsed 
during landslide incident at around 4.30 A.M. on 20-08-2022. 
In Kangra district, a flash flood incident occurred at gagal Khas village at 
around 6.38 A.M one person was killed while another person killed in a

text:

separate incident of flash flood at Kuthed village of shahpur tehsil at around 
8.18 A.M. 
In wake of heavy rainfall warning, District Administration Kullu has 
ordered to close all schools (government and private) including the 
Anganwadi Centres throughout the district. 
Even District Administration Mandi has ordered the closure of all the schools 
including the Anaganwadi Centres in Mandi District. Dharampur area of 
Mandi has also been submerged by flooding water. Landslide at Pandoh in 
Mandi District has also blocked the Chandigarh-Manali national highway-21. 
In Kangra district, the Chakki rail bridge along at Kandwal in Kangra district 
along Pathankot -Jogindernagar rail track has also been washed away with 
this now the reail connectivity has been suspende d till the time new bridge 
is not constructed or old bridge is not repaired. 

5. Flash Flood triggered due to cloudburst at Manali (Distt. Kullu): 
A flash flood triggered by cloudburst in seri nullah near the south 
portal of Atal tunnel, Rohtang damaged some machinery. Officials from 
project Yojak of Border Roads Organisation (BRO) said a contractor was 
engaged in some civil works close to the Seri nullah when flash flood caused 
damages to the machines. Three tractors and five other machines, including 
earth movers, were damaged or buried in the debris. No human loss was 
reported in the incident. Sources said the contractor was engaged in 
excavation with heavy machineries here. Besides machines, some damage to 
the infrastructure was also reported. BRO officials are assessing the loss. As 
Atal tunnel is situated very far from the nullah, there was no loss of 
infrastructure of the tunnel and highway. Vehicular movement across the 
tunnel was normal. However, a wooden footbridge was washed away in the 
nullah, which is a tributary of Beas River. A bridge connecting Solang village 
of Manali was swept away by the flooded river, leaving villagers stranded. 
Villagers said a permanent motorable concrete bridge has been sanctioned 
for the village more than a decade back but work on the bridge had stopped 
a long back. 

6. Heavy rain triggers falsh floods at Sangla valley in Kinnaur district 
near China Border:-

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2022
text:
Page No. 23 

The flashflood damaged the road in the vaillage besides crops in 
adjoining fields. It’s rare that a flashflood occurs in the cold desert region 
that receives scanty rain. Flashfloods in cold desert areas are rare. 
Fortunately, the flooding did not cause any damage to life, on 18 -07-2022. 
There are reports that a few houses were damaged and four vehicles are 
stuck in the debris. The flashflood also damaged farm land, a footbridge and 
the cremation ground at Chango, another village on the China border. No 
loss of life was reported. Rain triggered floods in Kinnaur ’s Malling Nullah, 
damaging the strategic road connecting Reckong Peo to Kaza in Spiti valley. 

7. Flash flood incident occurred in Chamba district: 
Heavy rains and subsequent landslides have thrown normal life 
completely out of gear in Himachal Pradesh with reports of three people 
feared drowned in Chamba district after a flash flood. Three villagers are 
missing while eight foot bridges, six watermills and one cowshed washed 
away in a flashflood in the Dharedi and Khodi villages of Chamba district on 
Sunday afternoon. According to information provided by the district 
emergency operation centre (DEOC) Chamba, those missing have been 
identified as Roshan Lal of of Khodi village, Konata Devi and Surender both 
of Dharedi village. Flashflood swept the villages around 3pm.

text:
8. Landslide incident at Sirmour district: 
Five members of a family were killed while another was seriously 
injured after their house collapsed due to landslide following heavy rainfall 
at Khijwari village under Raast Pancha yat in Ronhat area in Sirmaur district 
during wee hours on Monday. Apple orchards in Koti panchatyat of Ronhat 
area have also suffered extensive damage due to landslides and heavy rains. 
Chief M inister Jai Ram Thakur has condoled the deaths. He said the st ate 
government has directed the district administration to provide relief to the 
affected people. He said that every possible assistance would be provided to 
affected people. DDMA said that incident occurred during the wee hours on 
25-09-2022 when the house collapsed all of a sudden due to landslide. 
Rescue team could safely pull only one injured out of debris while the bodies 
of five others were retrieved from the debris. At the time of incident, family 
of Pradeep Kumar was sleeping inside the house. Pradeep Kumar is seriously 
injured in the incident and is admitted at the hospital for treatment. Those

killed have been identified as his wife Mamta (27), his daughters - Ishita (8), 
Aerang (2) and Alisha (6) and his niece Ankisha (7) died on the spot. 
Ramesh Si ngta, a resident of Koti Bounch panchayat said that 
landslide and heavy rain have also caused extensive damage to apple 
plantation in Koti area. Traffic has also come to a complete standstill due to

road repair is likely to take some time and till then people going towards the 
district headquarters and development block Sangrah will have to travel

Preparatory measures taken to prevent/reduce losses from disasters during this 
period: 
 The State government was well prepared for monsoons, and a video -
conference with all the DCs was held on 16th of June, 2022 under the 
Chairmanship of Principal Secretary (Revenue). 
 State hade released funds under SDRF to Deputy Commissioners and Line 
Departments to tune of Rs. 234.8083 Crore (Rs. 233.8083 allocated through 
treasury + Rs. 1.00 Crore through Bank Account to DC Kullu) in different 
heads (Copy enclosed). 
 QRTs were constituted for search and rescue in districts. 
 The State machinery was fully activated, and relief and restoration work was 
carried out round the clock. The situation in all the twelve districts was 
monitored constantly. 
 The DEOCs were monitoring and reporting incidents/losses and damages 
regularly and the State EOC generated cumulative loss reports on daily basis.

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2022
text:
Page No. 25 

 As a preparatory measure the NDRF was prepositioned at Mandi and Nurpur 
(Kangra). 
 The services of NDRF were availed at Rampur, Shimla, Baddi, Nalagarh, and 
Sirmaur. 
 Large number of machinery was deployed to clear the roads. 
 In Tehemerge Challenge Project, We have provided 3 Life buoys for Mandi, 
Kangra and Bilaspur district for Search and Rescue. One Drone provided to 
District Mandi for aerial survey. 
 Essential services like electricity and water were restored wherever damages 
had taken place. 
 Early warnings were disseminated regularly as and when received from IMD 
and CWC. 
 State has provided 23 Nos. Landslide sensors for Sirmour, Mandi, Kangra and 
Kinnuar District for Landslide Monitoring. 
 Search and Rescue (SAR) operations were executed promptly. 
 Do’s and Don’ts were broadcasted through AIR, TV, Print and Other 
electronic media. 

On account of the widespread damages and loss across the State, the Hon’ble 
Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh, Sh. Jai Ram Thakur held a video conference 
with all the DCs on 20th of August, 2022.

Extent of damages: 
The damages are detailed here under: 
1. Human lives lost: During this monsoon season 418 peoples lost their 
lives due to flash floods, landslides , ligtining, fire and cloudbursts. Ex-
gratia payment @ Rs.4.00 Lacs per head in this regard has been 
assessed at Rs. 16.72 Cr. 220 people also died due to various other 
reasons in this period directly or indirectly related to monsoon as the 
same has been notified as Sate Specific Disaster and ex -gratia 
payment @ Rs. 4.00 lacs is being released by the State Government 
under SDRF. Total loss on this account has been assessed to tune of 
Rs. 16.72 Crore. (Annexure-I) 

2. Animals Husbandry : A Total 966 animals died; which includes sheep, 
goats, cows, horse s and buffaloes in a major incident of Flash Flood, 
that happened at Shimla . In district. O ther infrastructure related to 
animal husbandry suffered a loss of Rs. 0.15 Crore. In this season, the 
loss has been assessed as Rs. 0.72 Crore.

4. Damage to roads: 
 Roads are life lines of the S tate as there are virtually negligible 
modes of alternate transport. The economy of S tate which comprises 
mainly tourism and horticulture is highly dependent upon road 
infrastructure. Himachal Pradesh has vast network of roads, which 
comprises 40000 km. of State Roads and 3017 km. of National 
Highways. The monsoon season has played havoc with road 
infrastructure this year. Extensive damages to the roads have been 
inflicted by way of landslides , damages to the various structures like 
Retaining walls, Breast walls, Cross drainage works, Bridges, besides 
heavy damage to the pavement/riding surface. It is mainly attributed 
to the mountainous/steep terrain and fragile Geological strata in most 
part of the S tate triggering landslides. The climate change/global 
warming has resulted in non uniform distribution of rains with very 
high intensity rainfall in localized areas thus, aggravating the extent of 
damages to road infrastructure. As a result , a number of road 
stretches, culverts and other structures have been washed away 
especially in Districts of Chamba, Kullu, Shimla, Kinnaur & Bilaspur. 
The department has deployed adequate number of various types of 
machinery including excavators, tippers, dozers and manpower as per 
requirement to restore the traffic in shortest possible time to provide 
relief to the general public at large. Nearly 23905 km of road leng th 
has been adversely affected. Due to flash flood and landslide, the 
PWD Infrastructure i.e. Roads, Bridges and culverts ha ve been 
severely damaged during the current Mo nsoon se ason. The total 
losses on this account have been assessed as Rs. 1013.52.Crore 
(Annexure-III). The damaged road infrastructure has been restored 
immediately with the help of Government and private machinery in 
order to avoid inconvenience to public. The permanent restoration 
work is still in progress.

5. Damage to Irrigation and water supply schemes: 

 Irrigation & Public Heal th Department is maintaining 95 26 
Water Supply, 2669 Irrigation, 97 Urban and 33 sewerage schemes in 
Rural and Urban areas of the State, The department is also protecting 
the flood prone areas to save culturable land, public and private 
property by providing flood protection measures in the shape of 
embankments, spurs and wire crates etc. 
 Heavy rain fall in various parts of the State during the period 
29-06-2022 to 28-09-2022 heavy loss to the Schemes of Jal Shakti 
Department in the State has been reported. Heavy rains have led to 
huge damages to the Water Supply, Irrigation, Sewerage and Flood 
Control works of the Department. A majority of water supply and 
irrigation schemes have sources in Khuds/ Nallah/ Rivers below high 
flood level. At many places heavy rains and cloud bursts triggered 
landslides and washed the Jal Shakti Department schemes and other 
common assets. 
 During the period from 29th June, 2022 to 28th September, 
2022 approximately total 16322 schemes (9854 instances of 
damages in Urban & Rural Water supply schemes, 2189 instances of 
damages in Irrigation, 112 instances of damages in sewerage 
schemes and 177 Flood Protection works) were damaged and tot al 
loss in terms of money has been estimated as Rs. 967.18 Crore. 
 In many places flash flood water entered in the campus of 
pump houses resulting in silting of pump houses, Treatment plants, 
pumping machinery etc. In some places Gravity Mains/Rising mains 
have also been washed away/damaged due to landslides This 
necessitated repair/cleaning of pumping machinery, cleaning /de -
silting of Pump Houses & other structures. 
 Being essential service first priority has been given to restore 
Water Supply and Sewerage Schemes in a time bound manner and all 
damaged water supply and sewerage schemes have been restored 
temporarily out of the available resources of the department. Pipes 
damaged due to heavy rains/ landslides have been replaced out of

on-going schemes. 
In order to repair /restore the damaged Water Supply and

spent out of the funds available for Operation and Maintenance of 
schemes/Capital Works for the year 2022 -23 and so far a liability of 
approximately Rs.175.00 Crores is outstanding.

6. Damage to Agriculture Crops: 
 Himachal Pradesh is a relatively small state in area and population 
and is geographically different from most Indian states in the plains. The 
State lies between 30˚22’40” and 33˚12’ 20” north latitude and 75˚45’ 
55” and 79˚04’20” east longitude. Himachal Pradesh has relatively 
abundant water resources from major five river systems, mostly 
originating from glaciers. The five major river basins cover around 90% 
of the geographical area. The surface water resources of these river 
systems are perennial, origin ating from glaciers, and the flow is further 
augmented by run -off from the downstream catchments. Most glaciers 
are small in size with length of 2 -25 km and accumulation zone of 2 -4 sq 
km. Due to the adverse effect of global warming phenomenon, constant 
recession phenomenon is recently hastening in these glaciers. 

Climate and Agro-ecological Zones 
 Climatically, Himachal Pradesh is different from most plain 
states in India. In the State, three seasons such as winter season 
(October to February), Summer s eason (March to June) and Monsoon

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2022
text:
Page No. 30 

season (July to September) are there. However, due to wide range in 
altitude, the climate of the State varies from sub -humid tropical 
(Elevation 350-1000 m) in the southern low tracts, warm and temperate 
(Elevation 1001 -1,500 m), cool and temperate (Elevation 1,501 -2,500 
m), and cold alpine and glacial (Elevation 2,501 - 6,975 m) in the 
northern and eastern mountain ranges. 
Damage caused to Agricultural crops of Kharif, 2022 season due to 
heavy rainfall: 

 During this monsoon period the percent departure of rainfall 
as per reports of Metrological Center Shimla is-3% up to 28th September, 
2022 below the normal rainfall in the state which indicates the Normal 
rainfall. About 20% of area is sown in the month of April -May whereas 
80% of area is sown in the month of June which is a peak Kharif sowing 
period. Due to normal rains in most part o f the state, the sowing could 
almost be done on time. However, during the month of Aug, 2022, there 
was heavy rainfall in some pockets of the state and standing Kharif crops 
particularly Maize & Vegetables crops were affected and Agriculture 
land was also washed away. As per assessment, the total area of 6,808 
Hectares was damaged and 294 Hectare land was washed away.The 
total damage including Crops, agriculture land, in terms of money value 
has been assessed around Rs. 72.22 Crore and 1.10 Crore of Land Lo ss.

7. Damage to Horticultural Crops: 
 Horticulture is an important sector of economic development 
in the S tate, which is contributing around 5000 crore towards S tates 
economy. It has a capacity to generate more income and 
employment per unit area. Fruit crops occupy about 2.29 lakh Ha 
area in the State. Apple, Mango, Citrus and other stone fruits are 
major fruit crops grown in the S tate and constitute about 83 % of 
total fruit production. Apple is th e dominating fruit crop of the S tate 
occupying about 48% of the total area under fruits & about 76.50 % 
of the total production and the State earned its name as “Apple State 
of India” is marching forward as “Fruit bowl of India”. About 5 lac 
families are directly or indirectly involved in the Horticulture 
primarily fruit production & its allied activities viz Bee Keeping, 
Mushroom production, Floriculture and Fruit processing. St ate 
economy is likely is shoot up in a big way as far as Horticulture 
industry is concerned with the launching of World Bank -aided-HP 
Horticulture Development Project and Asian Development Bank 
aided HP Sub -Tropical Development Project worth Rs. 1134.00 crore 
and Rs. 1688.0 crore respectively in which specific emphasis is to be 
given for High Density Plantation of various crops, creation of ample 
water resources through available means & strengthening of 
infrastructure facilities which are considered to be vital for 
promotion of horticulture in the entire State. 
 During the past couple of years , the S tate is witnessing 
natural fury/ calamities at intermittent intervals particularly losses 
being inflicted during the monsoon season resulting thereby the 
fluctuating production and productivity of fruit crops. Major losses 
generally inflicted during the mo nsoon season are losses in the form 
of mortality of young nursery plants due to constant water 
stagnation, partial damage to the twigs of fruit trees, landslides in 
various areas, quantitative and qualitative losses. Qualitative losses 
are more oftenly hig h due to appearance of various diseases in 
general as due to excessive rains diseases spread in alarming 
proportion thereby affecting the marketing of the produce. Size and

torrential.

during rainy season were Rs. 5.18 Crores (Annexure - VI)

Chapter -1 
State Profile 
Physical Location: 
Himachal Pradesh is predominantly a 
mountainous State located in North – West 
India. It shares an international border with 
China. The State has highly dissected 
mountain ranges interspersed with deep 
gorges and valleys. It is also characterized 
with diverse climate that varies from semi 
tropical in lower hills, to semi arctic in the 
cold desert areas of Spiti and Kinnaur. 
Altitude ranges from 350 meters to 6975 
meters above mean sea level. It is located 
between Latitude 30 O 22’.40” N to 33 O 
12’.20” N and Longitude 75 O 45’.55” E to 
79O 04’.20” E. 
Demography: 
Population of Himachal Pradesh is 68.56 lakh persons as per the Census 
report for the year 2011. 89.01% of the total population inhabits 20,604 villages in 
the rural areas of the State. These villages are sparsely distributed across the 
State having population density as low as 1 -2 persons per square kilometer in the

m above mean sea level and includes areas such as the upper parts of 
Pachhad and Renuka in Sirmaur district, Chachiot and Karsog tehsils of Mandi 
district and upper parts of Churah tehsil of Chamba district.

Geology & Geomorphology: 
Himachal Pradesh with its complex geological structures presents a 
complicated topography with intricate 
mosaic of mountainous ranges, hills and 
valleys. Composed of recent Alluvium, 
Shiwalik hills are made up of rocks such as 
sandstone, shale and clay that came into 
existence during the Eocene, Mioc ene and 
Pliocene period. 
The central part that extends from Chamba 
district in the north to Shimla district in the 
south is mainly represented by Jatog group 
of rocks which originated in middle 
Proterozoic period. In the north eastern 
portion unclassified Granites borders the 
central part in between Kullu, eastern 
Shimla, Lahaul -Spiti and parts of Kinnaur 
district. The eastern greater Himalaya 
presents the Triassic formation which is found in Kaza tehsil of LahaulSpiti district. 
The oldest rocks are Granites found atJeori -WangtuandBandel near Largi in Kullu 
district. These granites date back to a stage of the crust at a time when India was 
located 8000 Km southwest of its present position.

The climate varies across the state with the 
altitude. In the southern low tracks between an 
altitude of 400 -900 it is hot sub humid type, 
between 900 -1800m altitude warm & temperate, 
between 900 -2400 m cool & temperate, cold 
alpine & glacial above 2400 -4800 m altitude. 
Bilaspur, Kangra, Mandi, Sirmour, and Una 
districts experience sub tropical monsoon, mild 
and dry winter and hot summer. Shimla district 
has tropical upland type climate with mild and dry 
winter and short warm summer. Chamba district 
experiences, humid subtropical type climate 
having mild winter, long hot summer and moist all 
season. Kullu district experience mainly humid 
subtropical type of climate with mild winter moist 
all season, long hot summer and marine. During 
the period from January to February heavy 
snowfall in higher re aches create conditions for 
low temperature throughout the state making it 
unpleasant and series of western disturbances

Chapter – 3 
Brief Summary of Damages and Losses 
Major Disaster Events that occurred in State of Himachal Pradesh 
1. Damage on Kullu District 

Due to incessant rainfall which started in the district on 8 th July and 
relentlessly continued with same inten sity for more than 60 hours, major river 
valleys of the district i.e. Beas, Parbati, Sainj, Tirthan and Banjar valleys 
experienced devastating floods on 9 th, 10 th and 11 th July. Although there were 
minor isolated incidents of cloudbursts/flash floods but t he major damage was 
caused due to complete severe flooding of the entire valleys due to this 
incessant rainfall. Around 2600 landslides (as per preliminary reports) have 
been reported from across the district, out of which 300 are major landslides. 
There h as been massive loss of public infrastructure as well as private 
properties in the district due to these devastating floods, assessment of which is 
still going on and may be revised later. As per the data reported by various 
departments of the State Govern ment, there has been loss of 15pprox.. Rs 332 
crores (which doesn’t include the damages of NHAI) by way of damage to 
Roads, Water Supply and Irrigation schemes, electricity lines, 
horticulture/agriculture and other public institutions/buildings (a complete break-
up of the same is enclosed with this document). Around 23 bodies have been 
recovered so far in Kullu and downstream districts, which were either due to 
people having been washed away in the flood or getting buried under landslides. 
In addition, some persons are still reported to be missing and exact numbers 
can be ascertained only after the connectivity is completely restored in the entire 
district. 
Further, as per initial assessment, around 422 houses have been 
damaged fully while 462 have been dama ged partially. In addition, around 150 
shops/dhabas/commercial establishments have also been damaged. 
Following are some of the major incidents/damages which need to be 
highlighted:

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2023
text:
Page No. 16 

(a) There has been unprecedented damage to certain areas of Sainj 
valley. Al most 60 houses/commercial buildings/shops of main Sainj 
market got completely washed away due to flooding on 10 th and 11 th 
July. The connectivity has been severely affected as many bridges/foot 
bridges across the Sainj river have been damaged/washed away which 
has completely cut off around 6 Gram Panchayats of the valley. Some 
photographs of the damage are enclosed with this report. 
(b) Approximate 60 houses/shops/commercial establishments in Parla 
Bhunter area in Beas valley got completely washed away due to 
flooding of Beas river. The main bridges of the Beas river i.e. Akhara

Chapter – 4 
Preparatory Measures 
Preparatory measures taken to prevent/reduce losses from 
disasters during Monsoon Period 

Monsoon season brings a lot of challenges to the state and causes wide spread 
damages and losses. In order to reduce loss of human life and property, the State was 
well prepared to deal with the situation and had taken a lot of measures. Some of the 
steps taken have been elaborated in the succeeding paras. 
State Wide Mega Mock Drill 

The HP State Disaster Management Authority successful organized mega mock 
drill on Fl ood and Landslide conducted on 08.06.2023. The collaborative efforts and 
coordination displayed during the drill reflect a significant step towards unified disaster 
preparedness and response. By involving the National Disaster Management Authority 
(NDMA), various stakeholder departments, and response agencies, the exercise 
demonstrated the importance of working together during crises. 

The simulation of 60 different sites across the state in the mock drill provided a 
comprehensive and realistic approach to testing disaster response capabilities. This 
thorough assessment helped identify areas of improvement and strengths in the 
disaster management plan, contributing to more effective preparedness in the future. 

Some of the key aspects that were assessed and highlighted during the mock 
drill include: 
1. Effective Coordination and Collaboration: The success of the mock drill was 
attributed to the seamless coordination and collaboration among all participating 
agencies and stakeholders. This shows that working toge ther is essential in 
disaster management scenarios. 

2. Importance of Preparedness: The mock drill underscored the significance of 
regular preparedness initiatives. Being well -prepared and conducting such drills 
can enhance the response capacity during actual disasters. 

3. Communication Systems: The drill emphasized the need for robust 
communication systems that can function effectively during a crisis. Efficient

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2023
text:
Page No. 25 

communication is crucial for coordinating responses and disseminating 
information. 

4. Public Awareness and Participation: The drill stressed the importance of 
educating the public about disaster preparedness, evacuation procedures, and 
safety measures. Public participation and awareness can significantly improve 
overall response and safety. 

5. Resource Allocation and Management: The exercise exposed the importance of 
proper resource allocation and management. Adequate deployment of 
personnel, equipment, and relief materials can have a significant impact on 
response effectiveness and minimize casualties and damages. 

6. Multi-Agency Response: The mock drill highlighted the necessity of integrating 
efforts from various departments, including police, fire services, medical teams, 
and NGOs, to optimize disaster management strategies. A coordinated multi -
agency response is vital for handling large-scale disasters effectively. 

7. Evacuation Procedures: The mock drill involved government offices and schools 
conducting evacuation drills in their respective premises. This helped identify 
areas for improvement, such as identi fying safe evacuation routes and 
addressing potential bottlenecks to ensure swift and safe evacuations. 

Overall, the successful mock drill has proven to be an essential learning 
experience and a valuable tool for enhancing the state ’s disaster preparednes s 
and response capabilities. Implementing the lessons learned from the drill will 
undoubtedly strengthen the disaster management plan and improve overall 
resilience in the face of future emergencies

text:
Introduction: 
The State of Himachal Pradesh forms a part of the North -western Himalaya and is 
environmentally fragile and ecologically vulnerable. The occurrence of natural hazards 
emanating from the effects of climatological variations is a matter of immediate concern to the 
State of Himachal Pradesh, as every year the state experiences the fury of nature in various 
forms, like cloudbursts, flash floods, landslides, earthquakes, snow avalanches, droughts, etc. 
The fragile ecology of the mountain state, coupled with large variations in physio -climatic 
conditions, has rendered it vulnerable to the vagaries of c limate and natural disasters. 
Physiographically, the State has been divided into three broad units: the Lower or Outer 
Himalaya, the Middle Himalaya, and the Higher or Great Himalaya, and each unit is 
susceptible to different types of hazards depending upon the lithology, soils, and local climatic 
variations. 
Due to the diverse topography of the area, the flood problem in the state is largely 
isolated in nature. The monsoon, apart from acting as the lifeline in the young, lofty, and 
fragile mountain belt of the Himalaya, becomes a potential cause for disturbing slope stability, 
inflicting heavy loss of life, and damaging Government, private, and public property. High 
monsoon rains in the areas of the Shiwalik and Lower and Mid Himalayan ranges cause 
extensive floods during the rainy season. In the upper reaches of the Beas and Satluj valleys, 
the main problems are flash floods and bank erosion because of the steep slopes of rivers 
and High River flows due to heavy rains. Often, flash floods caused by cloudbur sts and 
temporary blockages of the river channels have also been observed. Extremely high -intensity 
rainfall events over a short period of time, or ‘cloudbursts, as they may be called, are a natural 
phenomenon in the Himalaya and have been found to be a do minant factor in causing 
extensive damage in different parts of the State during the monsoon period every year. 
During the current monsoon period of 2023, the State witnessed very heavy damage 
due to high precipitation on July 20, 2023, resulting in a loss of more than 6,000 crore to the

document_title: HP SDMA State Memorandum of Loss and Damage Monsoon 2023
text:
Page No. 30 

Government exchequer and a heavy loss of 182 precious human lives in different parts of the 
State. Chamba, Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, and Solan were the worst affected districts of the State 
that suffered heavy losses in life and property. 
Rainfall Trend Analysis in Himachal Pradesh 
In order to supplement the view of heavy precipitation during 2023, the rainfall 
analysis for the state of Himachal Pradesh was carried out using the available IMD 
data from 2014 -2023 during the perio d April to August each year. The rainfall data at 
five locations Mandi, Shimla, Bhuntar, Kangra and Kalpa in district Kinnaur has been 
used to validate and to quantify the rainfall data at these locations in H.P. Based on 
the analysis carried out, the following inferences were made: 
 A large variation was recorded in the summer precipitation during the period 
2014-2023 i.e in April 2023, the rainfall recorded was on higher side in 2023 
than the preceding years. In April 2014 (33.00mm) where as in 2023 it in creased 
to 185.20 mm at Mandi. 
 Likewise in May 2014, the rainfall recorded at Mandi was 76.50 mm (2014)

Damage Assessment 
The broad damage assessment was carried out physically based on the loss of 
infrastructure, land use /land cover, human lives, etc. However, an attempt was made to make 
use of the satellite data in mapping the area in terms of the damage and loss assessment. In 
view of the large affected area, initially the mapping was taken up for Kullu,Mandi, Sirmour, 
,Solan,Shimla and Chamba districts of Himach al Pradesh which were worst affected districts 
in terms of damage. 
Kullu is one of the important districts of the state, best known for its tourism potential. 
Beas is the major river system of the area that drains into the Indus River System and runs in 
almost north south directions before it enters Mandi district. The other important tributaries of 
the Beas are the Paravti, Jiwa, and Sainj, which join it mainly on its left bank. As far as the 
Beas basin is concerned, it has a history of damage in the past. Based on the historical 
analysis carried out in the district under the IHCAP program, 44 flood events have been 
identified between 1950 and 2014 (with >5000 casualties reported). Some of the extreme 
events that occurred were in 1959, 1971, 1978, 1985, 198 8, 1989, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 
and 2013. Most of them occurred during the monsoon season due to high intensity rains 
(cloudbursts) or longer duration rainfalls (monsoons), and Kullu is the most affected district in 
Himachal Pradesh. Based on the data ana lysis and interpretation carried out, the Beas 
catchment has a higher risk of flooding in comparison to the other catchments because of 
their topographic locations, geomorphic set -up, and infrastructure and land use land cover 
likely to be affected in case of any flood event. The past history of cloud burst events when 
plotted for different districts of Himachal Pradesh also reveals that the Kullu districts have 
witnessed the maximum number of cloud burst events and are thus highly prone to such 
events in t he future, also because of the climatic variations over the Himalayan region. The

text:

precipitation data plotted in Kullu district over the past decades also reveals that during the 
monsoon period, more precipitation occurs in July than in August. 
Likewise, Mandi, Sirmour,Solan, Shimla and Chamba districts of Himachal Pradesh, 
the Mandi distrc forms part of the Beas river basin, whereas in Sirmour, the Yamuna and its 
tributaries like Giri, Bata etc. are the predominant rivers which contributes the Yanmua ri ver 
system. In the Solan district, the drainage system is mainly characterised by the presence of 
tributaries like Ashwani, and Gambhar etc. The Shimla district the drainage system is well 
developed with left bank of Satluj shares boundary with the adjoin ing districts besides the 
Pabbar as the predominant tributary of the district. The Shimla hills are also the water divide 
of Indus and Ganges river system in the country.

Observation based on pre- and post-satellite data analysis 
 In some areas of the Beas basin downstream of Manali, cloud -free satellite data was 
accessible, thus that data was used for the comparison analysis. The pre -disaster data 
was acquired from the IRS LISS IV images for the months of October and November 
2021–2022; the post -disaster data was taken from the images for the days of 22 –23 
July 2023. 
 According to the investigation, the Beas River's riverbanks sustained the majority of the 
damages due to the high water volume that resulted from the extremely heavy 
precipitation that fell between July 9 and July 11, 2023. 
 It has also been noted that the main contributor to destruction was the river's altered 
path brought on by the high water level, which caused the Beas to follow its Palaeo 
courses in the majority of locations downstream of Manali along either bank. 
 In the Kullu district, a total of 217 landslides have been recorded, covering a total area 
of 198 ha, while in the Mandi district, a total of 142 landslides have been seen, 
covering a total area of 100 ha. 
 The Mandi-Kullu highway's overall road damage has been calculated to be 49 km in 
the Manali-Pandoh segment. 
 Using visual interpretation approaches, the pre - and post -disaster damage scenarios 
have been mapped and are displayed in the Figures and tables that are attached 
below. 
 The temporal study would support the assessment of the physical damages made 
during the current monsoon season utilizing the most recent technical tools. 
Limitations: 
 Space data is extremely helpful for conducting temporal analyses, but gathering high -
quality, cloud -free data in the Himalayas during the monsoon season is extremely 
challenging.

State Profile 

Physical Location: 
Himachal Pradesh is predominantly a mountainous State located in North – West 
India. It shares an international border with China. The State has highly dissected 
mountain ranges interspersed with deep gorges and valleys. It is also characterized with 
diverse climate that varies from semi tropical in lower hills, to semi arctic in the cold 
desert areas of Spiti and Kinnaur. Altitude ranges from 350 meters to 6975 meters above 
mean sea level. It is located between Latitude 30 O 22’.40” N to 33 O 12’.20” N and 
Longitude 75O 45’.55” E to 79O 04’.20” E. 

Figure 1.1Digital Elevation Model, H.P. 
Demography: 
Population of Himachal Pradesh is 68.56 lakh persons as per the Census report for 
the year 2011. 89.01% of the total population inhabits 20,604 villages in the rural areas of 
the State. These villages are sparsely distributed across the State having population density 
as low as 1-2 persons per square kilometer in the remote and tribal area of Lahaul & Spiti. 
Hamirpur district has largest population density of 369 persons per square kilometer as 
against 123 persons per square kilometer for the whole State. Himachal Pradesh is one of 
the few states of the country where gender equality is an integral part of the social ethos as 
well as the overall development strategy. Female literacy is well above the national level 
and women employment is much higher than in most states of the country.

Administrative Units: 
In order to make the functioning smooth, the State is divided into twelve districts 
which are grouped in three Revenue Divisions i.e. Shiml a, Mandi and Kangra. There are 
81 Sub Divisions, 113 Tehsil, 73 Sub-Tehsil, 88 Development Blocks and 3615 
Panchayats. The State has very effective structure of PRI’s co mprising 12 Zila Parishads 
and 81 Panchayat Samitis. There are also 27 Municipal Councils and 29 Nagar 
Panchayats, besides 7 Cantonment Boards and 5 Municipal Corporations in the State. 
Topography: 
Topographically, the state can be divided into three zones: 
1. The Shiwaliks or Outer Himalayas: It covers the lower hills of Kangra, Hamirpur, 
Una and Bilaspur, lower parts of Mandi, Solan and Sirmour districts. Within this zone, 
altitude varies from 350 m to 1500 m. 

2. Inner Himalayas or mid-mountains:Altitude varies from 1500 m to 4500 m above 
mean sea level and includes areas such as the upper parts of Pachhad and Renuka in 
Sirmaur district, Chachiot and Karsog tehsils of Mandi district and upper parts of 
Churah tehsil of Chamba district. 

3. Alpine zone or the greater Himalayas:Has altitude above 4500 m above mean sea 
level and comprises areas of Kinnaur district, Pangi tehsil of Chamba district and area 
of Lahaul&Spiti district. 

Geology & Geomorphology: 
Himachal Pradesh with its complex geological 
structures presents a complicated topography 
with intricate mosaic of mountainous ranges, 
hills and valleys. Composed of recent 
Alluvium, Shiwalik hills are made up of rocks 
such as sandstone, shale and clay that came 
into existence during the Eocene, Miocene and 
Pliocene period. 
The central part that extends from Chamba 
district in the north to Shimla district in the 
south is mainly represented by Jatog group of 
rocks which originated in middle Proterozoic 
period. In the north eastern portion unclassified 
Granites borders the central part in between Kullu, eastern Shimla, Lahaul -Spiti and parts

Wangtuand Bandel near Largi in Kullu district. These granites date back to a stage of the 
crust at a time when India was located 8000 Km southwest of its present position.

snowfall in higher reaches create conditions for low 
temperature throughout the state making it unpleasant

Pre-monsoon Period 
The pre-monsoon period varies each year, and its impact on rainfall can differ based on 
several factors, including climate patterns and regional variations. 
Weather summary 
Precipitation activity in Himachal Pradesh in the month of March was weak on many days 
with four days of widespread vigorous activity. In the month of April, precipitation 
activity in state was weak on many days with three days of fairly widespread to 
widespread precipitation activity. In May month, state received four spells of moderate 
precipitation at few places. 
Monthly Precipitation and Departure 
Himachal Pradesh received excess precipitation (24%) in March month i.e. from 
01.03.2024 to 31.03.2024 and normal precipitation ( -1%) in the April month i.e. from 
01.04.2024 to 30.04.2024. The State received large deficient precipitation ( -73%) in May 
month i.e. from 01.05.2024 to 31.05.2024. Districts Bilaspur, Chamba, Hamirpur, Kangra, 
Kinnaur, Lahaul -Spiti, Shimla, Sirmaur, Solan and Una received large deficient 
precipitation whereas districts Kullu and Mandi received deficient precipitation. 
Pre-Monsoon Season Precipitation and Departure 
The state received normal ( -8%) precipitation in Himachal Pradesh in pre -monsoon 
season i.e. from 01.03.2024 to 31.05.2024. 9 districts of the state received normal 
precipitation. District Kullu received excess precipitation whereas Kinnaur and Solan 
received deficient precipitation during pre-monsoon season.

section_title: Rainfall data for month of August 2024:
text:
Rainfall data for month of August 2024: 
Precipitation activity in Himachal Pradesh in the month of August was weak to normal on many 
days with four spells of fairly widespread to widespread precipitation activity of active intensity. 
State has received normal precipitation(243.6 mm) which is 73 rd highest rainfall in the month of 
August for the period (1901 -2024) whereas highest rainfall was received in the year 1927(542.4 
mm). 
Year Precipitation Departure 
1927 542.4 111.2 
2024 243.6 -5 

Monthly precipitation and departure: 
The State received normal precipitation ( -5%) with 243.6 mm actual rainfall against 256.8 mm 
normal rainfall in the August month i.e. from 01.08.2024 to 31.08.2024. District Kangra has 
received highest rainfall amount viz. 654.8 mm while district Shimla has received highest 
rainfall departure (53%) against normal rainfall. Districts Shimla, Sirmaur and Bilaspur received 
excess rainfall whereas Districts Mandi, Kangra, Solan, Chamba and Una received normal 
rainfall; Districts Hamirpur, Kullu and Kinnaur received deficient rainfall and District Lahaul -
Spiti received large deficient rainfall.
